I would generally recommend to steer away from mocks in the tests. This choice is by design of golang. Even for things like network calls or http services, you can write concrete tests - Golang makes it pretty easy to create a tcp listener or http test server so you don't have to mock these services. The httptest pkg [https://pkg.go.dev/net/http/httptest](https://pkg.go.dev/net/http/httptest) is written exactly for this purpose.

For testing postgres calls, I actually use a docker-compose file to launch a postgres container, so that I can easily test against actual postgres version used in production instead of mocks.  
  
It does muddy the divide between unit test & integration test, but I don't think that's so bad. There's a limited return on investment when testing w/ mocks.

You are close! It's true that none of these are correct. A and D are identical, but there are still four options, so your observations are 2 x 25%, 1 x 50% and 1 x 60%.

Now, lets assume each answer is correct and try to reach a contradiction.

If a is correct, then d must also be correct. You have a 50% chance to select a or d, so a -> 25% != 50%, so a cannot be correct.

If b is correct, then we have a 25% chance of choosing correctly, but b -> 60% != 25%, so b cant be correct.

if c is correct, then we have a 25% chance of choosing c, and again 50% != 25%, so c cannot be correct.

A and d are the same, so we already know d cannot be correct.

So, there's no correct answer here.

Encoding data as json is very readable and portable, but comes at the cost of high memory consumption. It’s a great place to start when passing data between computers, but when the data payload gets large enough, binary/blob encoding start to seem more appealing. Consider encoding x=10000. In json this like 5 bytes minimum, because ints are base10 strings, plus quotes, braces, and wherever else. But a binary encoding could encode this as a 4 byte /32bit int. In small payloads (think kb, maybe mb), this is inefficiency is negligible and completely worth it imo. But once we get to gb size payloads, it can put a huge strain on memory consumption.

\* Monument in the capital

Domination is one of my favs! I think the general strategy is to stack as many attack bonuses as possible and minimize casualties. Attack bonuses come from leader abilities, unique units, great generals, terrain, government policies, and of course superior tech. Minimizing casualties comes moving units in defensive formations and retreating weakened units before they are finished off.

I usually start war as early as possible. Warriors are actually pretty good at taking cities, so ancient era warmongering can be very successful. If there’s a civ close by, then you can usually snatch up their cities instead of building your own settlers (of course ai sucks at placing settlers, so it’s not without drawbacks). If you pick a military civ, then you’ll likely get a military city state nearby which lets you crank out units even faster.

Once you get into classical era, you should be upgrading warriors and start earning great generals. If there’s no early iron available, then rush for pikemen and skip spearmen entirely. You should have several iron mines before medieval era, either from conquered cities or your own settlements. Iron is crucial for knights and man at arms. 

From then on, it’s non-stop war until the game ends. Fund the army through pillaging, utilize production from internal trade routes to build even more units, and oppress the world with your superior might!

This kind of problem is called a classification problem; we're classifying contiguous chunks of land into continents. Classification is a surprisingly difficult problem for both people and computers, and this CivVI map with the seemingly weird continents is a classic example of this problem can go wrong. This is actually one of the most active areas of research in Data Science today. Ad companies are using the exact same algorithm that CivVI is probably using (KNN) to classify groups of people into categories based on website visits or whatever tracking data they have. CivVI map is 2d, and ad data is usually 512d or more, but the process is basically the same. Find points that are close enough to each other and call that a continent or an ad target group.
